deep_why: The core challenge is predicting purchase behavior when different customer groups have fundamentally different buying patterns. The method automatically divides features into two groups: some guide the main prediction model, while others steer how that model adapts itself for each group. The soundness comes from a simple principle: if you let different features drive prediction separately from driving adaptation, you avoid forcing the model to optimize conflicting goals at once. When a feature tries to both predict directly and adjust model weights, the system sends mixed signals during learning. By partitioning the work, each feature set focuses on what it does best, letting the adaptation mechanism discover which groups truly exist in the data rather than guessing from prior assumptions about customer segmentation.

Synthetic data quality depends on how the data generation mirrors real-world patterns. This work compares two directions: generating diverse raw data first then labeling it (causal), versus embedding the target label in the prompt and generating specifically to match that label (anticausal). The principle underlying causal ordering is that forcing a language model to generate data backward from labels creates an artificial shortcut—the model learns to describe the label directly rather than the underlying features that caused it. Real data contains messy correlations and variations beyond what the label captures; anticausal synthesis skips that diversity. Models trained on causal synthetic data see richer patterns because the generation process matches how real data forms, making the trained models generalize better to unseen examples that contain the natural complexity that labels alone cannot capture.

The core issue is that large language models carry internal beliefs that can contradict external evidence when fact-checking. The method estimates what the model knows versus doesn't know through confidence signals, then adapts evidence retrieval based on those boundaries. The principle is that a model performs most reliably when it stays in its zone of actual knowledge; if it claims high confidence incorrectly (a known human bias), gathering evidence cannot override a false internal certainty. By treating the model's confidence as a signal for what evidence to fetch, and then using causal methods to isolate how internal knowledge influences reasoning, the system avoids cases where the model overrides correct evidence with wrong internal knowledge. This works because it separates the model's knowledge boundaries from its reasoning process, preventing false confidence from contaminating the fact-check result.

The problem is estimating causal effects in knowledge graphs where data is incomplete and entities influence each other. The approach reformulates this as two linked prediction tasks: filling missing attributes and estimating treatment effects while accounting for interference between connected entities. The principle is that if you handle missing data and interference together through a unified learned representation, you can estimate effects that remain valid even when the data is sparse. Graph methods work here because they explicitly model which entities affect which others; by letting information flow through the graph structure during learning, the system discovers interference patterns that affect causality estimates. Missing attributes get filled consistently with these relational patterns, so the final causal estimates account for the true dependencies rather than treating each entity in isolation or naively ignoring missing information.

Phishing websites try to mimic legitimate sites, so detection must recognize subtle differences in domain structure and content. The method combines large language models and traditional machine learning tools to classify domains as phishing or safe. The principle is that different model families capture different signals: traditional models learn from explicit structural features like domain age and certificate properties, while language models understand deceptive writing patterns and social engineering tactics embedded in site content. By comparing what each model type sees, the system builds robustness—if one model is fooled by a particular deception, another model trained on a different type of signal can catch it. This works because phishing involves multiple types of deception (technical spoofing plus human manipulation), and no single approach detects all variants equally well.

Sequential recommendation needs to guess what users will click next given their history. The method uses diffusion models (a generative approach that builds structure by gradually removing noise) while embedding both implicit information (learned user behavior patterns) and explicit information (known user-item interactions). The principle is that diffusion gradually reveals structure, so you can steer that unfolding process using explicit knowledge to avoid learning spurious patterns. Implicit signals capture what behaviors actually correlate with interest; explicit signals constrain the generation to only plausible user-item pairs. By conditioning the diffusion on both simultaneously, the model learns to extend sequences in ways that honor what it knows about real interactions while remaining open to novel discoveries. This avoids oversimplifying behavior into a single summary, preserving the temporal structure that makes sequential prediction work.

Causal learning is rapidly expanding with many algorithms but no consistent benchmarking standards, making it impossible to know which methods work best for which problems. The workshop aims to systematize benchmarks for causal methods, establishing agreed-upon datasets, evaluation metrics, and test scenarios. The principle is that scientific progress depends on reproducible, shared comparisons; without standardized benchmarks, each paper optimizes against different criteria, creating illusions of superiority rather than genuine advances. By defining benchmark tasks in causal discovery and causal inference consistently, the community can measure what each algorithm actually excels at and identify which problems remain unsolved. This works because it aligns incentives toward real algorithmic improvements rather than gaming evaluation metrics, enabling fair algorithm selection and guiding where future research should focus.

Academic search (finding papers to read, cite, or review) requires combining diverse signals: citation links, abstract content, and semantic similarity. The Scholar API provides a unified interface to multiple embeddings—some learned from deep models fine-tuned on citations, others computed via spectral methods on the citation graph structure. The principle is that different embeddings capture different notions of relatedness: citation-aware embeddings reflect what researchers actually build on, while spectral methods reveal hidden groups in the research landscape. By letting users combine embeddings flexibly, the system lets them optimize for their specific task: reviewers benefit from citation structure, authors seeking related work benefit from semantic similarity, funding agencies benefit from identifying emerging research clusters. This works because no single embedding captures all aspects of scholarly relevance simultaneously.

Machine unlearning tries to remove a person's data from a trained model without retraining from scratch, which is important for privacy. The fundamental challenge is measuring whether the influence truly disappeared—most datasets designed for this lack enough identity-specific variations to catch when a model generates false information instead of actually forgetting. The method establishes three measurable criteria: reducing how often the model mentions a specific person, removing their identity from generated captions, and maintaining overall caption quality. By creating a large dataset with multiple captions per person (some naming them, some not, some detailed versus summary), the evaluation can quantitatively check each criterion. This works because it forces unlearning methods to prove they actually erased identity information rather than just pausing brief outputs; the varied captions reveal whether models truly forgot or merely suppressed certain patterns.

The workshop focuses on graphs as a model for web-scale data (links, social networks, knowledge bases) and how to reason over them reliably. Modern graph methods combine structured graph reasoning with language understanding, but ensuring such systems remain interpretable and trustworthy at scale is difficult. The principle underlying reliable graph analytics is that transparent reasoning paths matter: users need to understand why the system recommended a person as reviewer, flagged content as misinformation, or identified a research trend. This works because graphs at web scale serve human ends—editorial decisions, policy recommendations, research guidance—where blind accuracy without interpretability creates risk. By grounding graph analysis in explainability and addressing social goals explicitly (misinformation detection, human-AI collaboration), systems can be both effective and aligned with real needs rather than optimizing only for numerical performance.

Bundle recommendation (suggesting sets of items together) is hard when bundles are new because models have no direct examples to learn from. The method mines user-item and bundle-item relationships to infer which users are likely interested in which new bundles, then uses contrastive learning to build robust representations that work in both cold-start and warm-start scenarios. The principle is that new bundles share items with popular ones; if you understand how users relate to individual items and how items compose bundles, you can predict interest in new combinations without direct training data. By comparing positive bundles (ones users actually want) against negative ones (similar but not chosen), the model learns what makes a bundle appealing relative to alternatives. This works because bundle preference is determined by item composition and user taste, both of which exist in the historical data even if specific bundles don't.

Taxonomy completion automatically places new concepts into a hierarchy by predicting which existing parent-child relationship they fit into best. The method improves this by generating harder negative examples during learning—instead of using random incorrect positions as negatives, it uses a diffusion model to synthesize increasingly difficult false placements. The principle is that learning improves when contrasts are meaningful; if the model only learns to distinguish true positions from obviously wrong ones, it remains brittle against ambiguous cases. By generating negatives that are semantically close to correct answers but still wrong, the model learns finer distinctions necessary for accurate placement. This works because the hardness of negative examples directly determines what boundaries the model learns; mixing easy and hard negatives teaches the model to discriminate subtle semantic differences between related concepts, making it robust to genuinely difficult classification decisions.

Sequential recommendation via diffusion models faces two problems: the generation process can drift (producing recommendations that stray from the user's actual preferences), and real data contains noise that corrupts the learning process. The method adds two fixes: using a transformer designed to extract user preference signals cleanly, and constraining the diffusion process to stay on a geometric surface that represents valid user-item relationships. The principle is that diffusion generates by gradually denoising, but without guidance this denoising can follow false patterns created by sparse data. By respecting the geometric structure of user-item space (where valid preferences form a low-dimensional surface), the diffusion stays anchored to realistic sequences even in high-dimensional settings. This works because user preferences follow natural clustering patterns; forcing the diffusion to move along these natural clusters rather than through empty space prevents drift and improves stability.

Social media shapes behavior through emotional contagion—when people see others' emotions, those emotions spread and influence their own responses. The talk analyzes this by detecting emotions in online text and tracing how they correlate with behaviors like polarization, engagement, and identity formation. The principle is that emotions act as carriers of social influence; when you measure the emotional tone of interactions, you can see how affect flows between people and populations. Different groups show different emotional signatures: in-group communication emphasizes shared joy and loyalty, while out-group interactions contain anger and dismissal, creating emotional barriers that drive polarization. This works because emotions are drivers of human attention and decision-making; by quantifying emotional dynamics, researchers can explain observed social phenomena (polarization, misinformation spread, group formation) as emerging from emotional processes rather than treating them as separate from how people actually think and decide.

Electronic health records contain vast information but it's scattered, redundant, and often irrelevant to specific medical predictions. The method rewrites raw records into summaries optimized for a particular clinical task (like predicting hospital readmission), then trains both the rewriter and the predictor end-to-end using synthetic guidance based on what features clinicians know matter. The principle is that not all health information equally informs every decision; a summary effective for predicting readmission differs from one useful for infection risk. By training the rewriter specifically to highlight features that improve prediction, the model learns what information to compress and what to preserve. This works because clinical knowledge about which factors drive specific outcomes can guide the learning process; synthetic labels built from domain expertise act as a compass, telling the model which records are well-rewritten, so it learns to extract signal rather than noise from the sparse, high-dimensional raw data.
